source.title: The Sharp Directions Are Against You: Curvature Analysis of Activation Steering
source.authors: Seyedarmin Azizi; Arya Fayyazi; Parsa Razmara; Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo; Souvik Kundu; M. Pedram

record.tranche_reason: The study tests activation-space steering and refusal outcomes using a curvature-based method rather than reproducing the original single-direction ablation procedure. It also evaluates negative-polarity steering as a jailbreak.
record.gate_note: The paper reports refusal-generation outcomes, benign-prompt false refusals, token-level anti-steer rates, and negative-steering jailbreak outcomes. The CAA exemplar and target-token choices are not recorded as results. It cites the original refusal-direction work, but cited results are not included.
record.test_reason: The study analyses curvature of CAA steering vectors and proposes 'sharp removal'. Its refusal vector is a CAA vector from 20 contrastive behavioural pairs, not the harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction V1 names. The paper reports this vector's cosine with the Arditi direction as 0.01–0.20, so the CAA rows measure a different vector. The Arditi direction appears only in Appendix J, to show sharp removal composes with other steering methods. It is a comparator for the authors' method, not a test of whether that direction mediates refusal. Negative-polarity steering deliberately induces compliance with the CAA and Hessian-derived vectors. It does not examine whether jailbreaks act by suppressing the refusal direction, and there is no training against ablation, so it does not bear on V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the steering-Hessian spectrum is strongly anisotropic and that its sharp eigen-directions reverse intended behaviour in all 36 conditions. The small sharp component of CAA drives most of the steered-versus-unsteered divergence in generation, and removing it beats CAA in 25/25 generation conditions. On refusal, CAA lowers safety on Qwen and Llama while sharp removal restores it. Sharp directions act as noise regardless of polarity: −v_sharp is the weakest jailbreak, −v_cleaned the strongest. They make no claim about the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction beyond using it as a vector their correction composes with.
record.recipe_differences: The study estimates a behavioral-loss Hessian and projects sharp components out of CAA or another steering vector. It does not reproduce the original all-layer, all-position ablation of the single harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports variation by model, layer, task, steering coefficient, sharp-subspace dimension, and refusal evaluator; Mistral refusal rates differ substantially between keyword detection and the GPT-4o-mini judge.

fits_no_version.finding: A CAA refusal vector built from 20 contrastive behavioural pairs, added at alpha 5.0, lowers harmful-prompt refusal. Qwen drops from 78% to 36–44% and Llama from 62% to 24–52%. Projecting out a 1–5%-energy Hessian sharp component restores refusal to 88–98% and 74–76%. This vector has cosine 0.01–0.20 with the Arditi direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contrastive (CAA) refusal steering vectors can be sign-inverted or destabilised by a small high-curvature component; their effect on refusal depends on removing it.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering along top Hessian eigen-directions of the refusal loss reverses intended refusal on 69–100% of inputs at the token level. In generation it causes near-total over-refusal (95–97%) or repetition loops.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High-curvature activation directions disrupt refusal behaviour indiscriminately, regardless of polarity.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says code and evaluation data will be released upon acceptance)
record.problems: The study covers three 7–8B instruct models and four behavioral tasks. It reports no error bars or confidence intervals for the listed refusal outcomes. Some refusal findings are reported as ranges across layers rather than per-layer values, and the Mistral keyword heuristic undercounts refusals relative to the LLM judge. The paper notes that its Hessian is local to alpha=1.0 and that transfer under distribution shifts is open.
record.rows_left_out: The paper gives further refusal and safe-prompt outcomes in flattened or figure-based plots without clearly assignable per-layer values in the text; these were not split into inferred model-layer rows. Other task results (sentiment, sycophancy, toxicity), PCA controls, curvature quantities, and the ambiguous Appendix J numerical comparison involving the Arditi direction were left out because they do not clearly measure versions V1–V8 as stated.

untested.parts: No ablation of the harmful-minus-harmless direction across layers and positions. Adding the Arditi direction is reported only as one comparator number in Appendix J. No capability check.
No analysis of whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction; no training against ablation.
No test of affine, cone or multi-direction refusal structure.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer.

missing.what: Adding the Arditi et al. refusal direction reaches 100% refusal without correction on Qwen L10 and Llama L15. Its sharp energy is about half of CAA's (0.44% vs 0.98%; 1.30% vs 2.61%), and its cosine with CAA is 0.01 and 0.20. Harmful-prompt set and alpha are not clearly stated. This is the only result on the V1 direction itself, but it is a comparator for the authors' method.
missing.locator: Appendix J, 'Complementarity with other steering methods'

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 and V3 links rest on treating the CAA refusal vector as the V1 direction. The paper's own cosine of 0.01–0.20 with Arditi's direction contradicts this, so all rows are relinked to none and the record's labels are dropped. The baselines are inconsistent: the Qwen refusal baseline is 78% in Fig. 3 but 82% in Fig. 7. The Qwen L10 CAA value is 44% in the k-sweep versus 36% in the prose. Refusal generation used alpha 5.0, while the Hessian was estimated at alpha 1.0. No error bars are reported for refusal results.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate the original single difference-in-means refusal direction at every layer and position, or establish that removing it eliminates refusals. It does not measure general capability broadly; its safe-prompt test is an over-refusal check.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
Tests negative-polarity activation steering as a jailbreak, not other attacks that suppress the direction. Does not train models against ablation.
Does not test whether refusal is better represented as an affine set, cone, or dominant direction plus additional refusal directions.
Does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
Evaluates separate model families but does not test whether one identified direction transfers across languages, variants, or from base to instruct models.
Does not vary refusal-training method or timing.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Qwen safe-prompt steering at alpha 1.0 and 2.0
reader_labels.reason: CAA increases false refusals on safe prompts from 4% to 16%, and at alpha 2.0 produces 53% full refusals; see r1–r4.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Llama safe-prompt steering and sharp-removal conditions
reader_labels.reason: On Llama, false-refusal rates under baseline, CAA, and sharp removal are all reported in the same 11–12% range; on Qwen sharp removal leaves 11% false refusals at alpha 1.0. These tests do not show a uniform effect of steering or correction on benign prompts; see r3, r6–r8.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: CAA refusal steering on AdvBench harmful requests
reader_labels.reason: CAA lowers refusal rates below baseline on Qwen and Llama, while sharp removal restores or exceeds baseline; this is not evidence that ablating the original single direction removes refusal; see r10–r13.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Mistral refusal steering, layer 12, GPT-4o-mini judge
reader_labels.reason: The judged full-refusal rate rises from a 52% baseline to 68% with CAA and 88% after sharp removal; see r14–r16.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Negative-polarity steering on Qwen jailbreak prompts
reader_labels.reason: Negative CAA and negative sharp-removed steering raise non-refusal to 68% and 80%, respectively, from 6% at baseline; see r17, r18, and r20.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Negative-polarity steering on Llama jailbreak prompts
reader_labels.reason: Negative CAA and negative sharp-removed steering mostly yield partial compliance, with only 2% and 3% full compliance; negative sharp-projection steering instead produces 100% refusal; see r21–r24.
